entries.question: When were the stars made?
entries.summary: Genesis 1:16-19 has God making the stars on the fourth day of creation, after the earth already existed. Job 38:4-7 pictures the 'morning stars' already singing together when God laid the earth's foundations, placing the stars before the earth.
entries.commentary: This contradiction plays out between genre registers, but it still sits awkwardly. Genesis 1 is a structured Priestly cosmogony with a clear sequence: earth on day three, luminaries including stars on day four. Job 38 is poetic speech, but the cosmological picture it paints has the stars (or angelic 'sons of God' associated with stars) already present and celebrating when the earth gets founded. Apologists commonly argue Job 38 is poetry and shouldn't be pressed for chronology, or that 'morning stars' there refers to angels rather than literal stars, pointing to the parallelism with 'sons of God' (bene elohim). That's not a bad move, and it's the line Gleason Archer and John Walton take. But the poetic/literal split doesn't eliminate the problem, because even if 'morning stars' means angels, the passage still presents stars as part of the cosmological furniture before the earth is founded. And the Genesis 1 sequence itself is a known ancient Near Eastern oddity. Mark Smith notes that the Priestly author is adapting a schema where the luminaries are deliberately demoted from their usual divine status, so they get delayed to day four as functional objects rather than beings. That is a subjective read, but the tension is real either way.
entries.scholarship: Mark S. Smith, The Priestly Vision of Genesis 1 (Fortress, 2010), pp. 83-85, on the demotion of luminaries. Nahum M. Sarna, Genesis (JPS Torah Commentary, 1989), pp. 8-9. John H. Walton, Genesis 1 as Ancient Cosmology (Eisenbrauns, 2011), pp. 104-119. Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties (Zondervan, 1982), pp. 60-61. Marvin H. Pope, Job (AB 15; Doubleday, 1965), pp. 293-294, on 'morning stars' in Job 38:7.

answers.answer: On the fourth day of creation, after the earth was made.
answers.answer_explanation: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. Genesis 1:1He made the stars also. And God set them in the firmament of the heaven.... And the evening and the morning were the fourth day. Genesis 1:16-19
Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? ... When the morning stars sang together. Job 38:4-7

commentary_out.commentary:
The tension here runs between two very different genre registers, and the resolution turns largely on how Job 38 is read. Genesis 1:14-19 is a structured Priestly cosmogony with an explicit sequence: dry land and vegetation on day three, then the luminaries — sun, moon, and 'the stars also' (we-et ha-kokhavim) — set in the firmament on day four, after the earth already exists. Job 38:4-7, by contrast, is divine speech from the whirlwind, cast in tight synonymous parallelism: 'Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?… when the morning stars (kokhevei voqer) sang together and all the sons of God (bnei elohim) shouted for joy?' The poetic structure places the stars among the celebrants present at the earth's founding, which on a flat chronological reading puts them before the earth — the reverse of Genesis 1.

The strongest harmonization, advanced by Gleason Archer and John Walton, makes two moves. First, genre: Job 38 is hymnic theophany, not a sequential creation account, and pressing its imagery for chronology mistakes its rhetorical purpose, which is to overwhelm Job with the inaccessibility of creation's origins ('Where were you?'), not to date the stars. The whole speech is a barrage of unanswerable questions designed to expose the limits of human knowledge, and the founding-of-the-earth imagery (architectural language — foundations, measuring line, cornerstone, 38:4-6) is metaphor drawn from human building, not a cosmological timetable. Second, referent: the parallelism 'morning stars // sons of God' strongly suggests that 'morning stars' is a poetic designation for the angelic host rather than literal astronomical bodies. Marvin Pope's Anchor Bible commentary notes that the pairing reflects the widespread ancient association of stars with divine beings (compare Isa 14:12, helel ben shachar, 'Day Star, son of Dawn,' and the astral deities of Ugaritic myth, where the divine assembly is regularly imagined among the stars). On this reading the verse is not asserting that physical stars were manufactured before the earth; it is depicting the heavenly court rejoicing at creation, and the chronological clash with Genesis 1 largely dissolves into figurative language.

The versional evidence reinforces that both registers were heard in the line from antiquity. The Old Greek of Job 38:7 reads hote egenethe astra ainesan me phone megale pantes angeloi mou — 'when the stars came into being, all my angels praised me with a loud voice.' The verb egenethe (aorist of ginomai, a third-person singular in the ordinary Greek concord by which a neuter-plural subject astra takes a singular verb) renders the first colon in astral terms, and on the lexical sense of ginomai ('come into being, be made') it favors a literal/created reading of the stars rather than a purely figurative angelic one; it is the second colon, 'all my angels' (pantes angeloi mou), that translates the Hebrew parallel 'sons of God' and supplies the part that supports the angelic association. The LXX thus splits the difference: it keeps astral language in the first colon while making the angelic identity explicit in the second, illustrating that ancient translators already heard both registers in the verse rather than collapsing them into one. The point cuts in both directions — it weakens the apologetic claim that 'morning stars' simply means angels, while confirming the broader ancient overlap of stars and divine beings.

This is a fair and largely persuasive harmonization, and it is why the status is partial rather than full contradiction. Two residual points keep the tension from fully evaporating. First, even granting the angelic reading, the passage still presents the heavenly beings (whether called stars or sons of God) as already in existence and active at the moment the earth is founded — which sits awkwardly with the Priestly insistence that the entire cosmos, heavenly bodies included, is created within the six-day frame, and with the later notion that the angelic host is itself a created order. Job nowhere narrates a creation of these beings; they are simply there. Second, the Genesis 1 placement of the luminaries on day four is itself a deliberate theological maneuver rather than a naive observation. Mark Smith argues that P intentionally demotes the sun, moon, and stars from the divine status they held throughout the ancient Near East (where they were astral deities), reducing them to functional timekeepers 'to separate day from night' and 'for signs and seasons' (Gen 1:14) — notably refusing even to name 'sun' and 'moon,' calling them only the 'greater' and 'lesser light.' That polemical demotion is precisely why they are introduced late, as manufactured objects. Job 38, working in an older and more comfortably mythopoeic idiom, still treats the astral/divine beings as primordial celebrants. Nahum Sarna's JPS commentary likewise stresses that the day-four placement is a calculated literary and theological choice within P's seven-day frame, not a chance ordering. So the two texts reflect different theological postures toward the heavenly bodies even if the genre argument neutralizes the surface chronology. Verdict: largely overstated/harmonizable on genre and the angelic referent, with a residual tension over the primordial status of the heavenly host.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Job 38 is hymnic-poetic theophany, not a creation chronology, and the parallelism of 'morning stars' with 'sons of God' (bene elohim) suggests the line evokes the angelic council rather than asserting a literal pre-earth manufacture date for stars. On that reading the genre convention and the figurative referent absorb most of the surface tension, though a residual cosmological mismatch with Genesis 1's day-four placement of the luminaries remains.

commentary_out.change_summary: Restored the singular LXX verb egenethe (Rahlfs) with ainesan, reframed the astral-creation point to rest on the lexical sense of ginomai rather than verb number, normalized the Hebrew transliteration to kokhevei voqer, and preserved all five citations. [hand-corrected post-audit]

issues.problem: The expanded commentary cites the Old Greek (LXX) of Job 38:7 as 'hote egenethesan astra, enesan me phone megale pantes angeloi mou.' The actual Rahlfs LXX text of Job 38:7 reads 'hote egenethe astra ainesan me phone megale pantes angeloi mou' — the verb is the SINGULAR egenethe (aorist passive 3rd sing.), not the plural egenethesan, and the praise verb is ainesan (from aineo), not 'enesan.' The commentary's own change_summary claims it 'Corrected the LXX verb to the plural egenethesan,' which is itself the error: the standard critical text has the singular. Presenting a non-standard verb form as the LXX reading and then resting a text-critical argument ('astra ... they came into being, were made,' plural agreeing with neuter plural astra) on it is a fabricated/incorrect linguistic claim.
issues.correction: Quote the LXX as 'hote egenethe astra ainesan me phone megale pantes angeloi mou' ('when the stars came into being, all my angels praised me with a loud voice'). Note that egenethe is grammatically singular with a neuter-plural subject (normal Greek concord), so the argument that the plural verb form proves a 'literal/created' reading should be dropped or reframed; the astral-creation sense rests on the lexical meaning of ginomai, not on a (non-existent) plural verb form.

issues.problem: The change_summary states a 'high-severity audit flag' instructed correcting the LXX verb TO the plural egenethesan. This documents the introduction of the erroneous form as if it were the fix, compounding the linguistic error in the commentary.
issues.correction: Reverse: restore the singular egenethe per Rahlfs/Ziegler and remove the claim that the plural form was a correction.

entries.question: When did God divide light from darkness?
entries.summary: Genesis 1:4-5 says God divided light from darkness on the first day of creation, before any celestial bodies existed. Genesis 1:16-19 then has God creating the sun, moon, and stars on the fourth day and using them to divide light from darkness.
entries.commentary: This one is almost self-refuting because both verses are inside the same chapter and turn on the same Hebrew verb — the Hiphil of b-d-l, 'to separate between the light and the darkness' — day one as the finite vayyavdel ('and [God] separated,' Gen 1:4) and day four as the infinitive lehavdil ('to separate,' Gen 1:18). Day one does the dividing. Day four does the dividing again, this time with the luminaries as the mechanism. Apologists like Archer usually argue that day one refers to primordial light (maybe God's own glory or some pre-solar cosmic light) and day four is just when God instituted the regular rhythm through the sun and moon. That's a workable reading if you assume Genesis 1 was composed as a single tight cosmology, but it isn't. Mark Smith and the mainstream of Pentateuchal scholarship recognize that the Priestly author is building a liturgical-cosmological structure in which days one through three create domains and days four through six fill them. That structural parallelism is why the 'dividing' gets repeated. The text isn't claiming two different acts of dividing in a unified timeline, it's the Priestly author using the same vocabulary to mark the correspondence between the creation of the environment (day 1) and the creation of the inhabitants of that environment (day 4). The problem is that once you read it as straight chronology, the text contradicts itself, and the ancient author almost certainly didn't care because the structure was the point.
entries.scholarship: Mark S. Smith, The Priestly Vision of Genesis 1 (Fortress, 2010), pp. 87-92, on the domain/inhabitants parallel structure. Gordon J. Wenham, Genesis 1-15 (WBC 1; Word, 1987), pp. 6-7. Claus Westermann, Genesis 1-11: A Continental Commentary (Fortress, 1984), pp. 112-114. Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties (Zondervan, 1982), pp. 60-61, for the two-phase harmonization.

answers.answer: On the first day of creation.
answers.answer_explanation: God divided the light from the darkness. And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day. - Genesis 1:4-5

And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night ... to divide the light from the darkness: and God saw that it was good. And the evening and the morning were the fourth day. - Genesis 1:16-19

commentary_out.commentary:
This is an unusual case because both verses sit within a single chapter and pivot on a single Hebrew root, b-d-l ('to separate, divide'), in the Hiphil stem. Day one reports a completed act: vayyavdel elohim bein ha-or u-vein ha-choshek, 'and God separated the light from the darkness' (Gen 1:4), and God then names the light Day and the darkness Night. Day four assigns the same function to the newly made luminaries: they are set in the firmament 'to give light upon the earth, and to rule over the day and over the night, and to separate (u-le-havdil) the light from the darkness' (Gen 1:18). The puzzle is plain: if the light/darkness division was accomplished and named on day one, before any celestial body existed, what is left for the sun and moon to divide on day four? The same verb governs both, once as a finite wayyiqtol (vayyavdel) and once as an infinitive of purpose (le-havdil), which makes the repetition unmistakable rather than incidental.

The traditional harmonization, run by Archer and many conservative commentators, posits two phases: day one introduces a primordial, non-solar light — sometimes identified with the divine glory or an undifferentiated cosmic luminescence — and day four institutes the regular, mechanically governed alternation of day and night through the sun and moon. This reading has ancient pedigree. The notion of a primordial light distinct from the sun appears in rabbinic tradition (the or ganuz, the 'hidden light' that b. Chagigah 12a says was created on day one and then stored away for the righteous in the world to come), and the difficulty of pre-solar light was felt across Second Temple literature (4 Ezra 6:38-41 dwells on the brightness commanded forth at the beginning of creation). As a piece of theology the primordial-light reading is coherent and old. As an account of what the text describes, it strains, because the verb and object are identical in both verses; the text does not say day four creates a new kind of light-cycle but that the luminaries perform the same dividing already reported in 1:4.

The more economical explanation, and the mainstream critical one, is literary-structural. Mark Smith, Gordon Wenham, and Claus Westermann all observe that Genesis 1 is organized as a deliberate two-panel framework: days one through three create the realms or domains (light/day, sky and sea, dry land with vegetation), and days four through six populate or govern those domains (luminaries to rule day and night, birds and fish, land animals and humans). Day four corresponds to day one precisely because the luminaries are the 'rulers' (the verb m-sh-l, 'to rule,' Gen 1:16, 18) installed in the light-domain established on day one. The repetition of the separating vocabulary is therefore not a claim about two distinct physical events on a single timeline but a literary signal of the day-1/day-4 correspondence. Wenham presents this framework as the key to the chapter's architecture; Westermann reads the luminaries' 'separating' as their ongoing governing function rather than a redundant re-creation of the day-one division. The polemical thrust reinforces the reading: by delaying the sun and moon to day four and assigning them a merely functional, subordinate role, P strips the great astral deities of the surrounding cultures of their divinity — refusing even to name them, calling them only the 'greater' and 'lesser light' (Gen 1:16) — while still acknowledging the obvious fact that it is the sun that now governs the day.

It is worth adding that the framework reading does not require denying that P thought light somehow existed before the sun; the ancient cosmology that produced this text plainly did distinguish light as a created reality (1:3) from the luminaries as later furniture (1:14-19), and that distinction is itself a marker of the chapter's pre-scientific astronomy rather than a covert two-phase apologetic. The day-one light is the cosmic condition that makes day and night possible; the day-four luminaries are the bodies installed to administer that already-instituted cycle. On the author's own terms the repetition is functional, not contradictory.

So the assessment depends on the question being asked. If one reads Genesis 1 as the carefully patterned liturgical cosmology its author composed — with its sevenfold rhythm, its refrains ('and God saw that it was good'), and its panelled symmetry — the repeated b-d-l language is intelligible and not self-contradictory; the structure is the point, and the author very likely was not narrating sequential natural history at all. If one insists on reading it as a strict chronological report, then the text does separate light from darkness twice, once with no luminaries and once with them, and that is incoherent. The contradiction is thus real under a flat-literal reading and dissolves under the literary reading the text's own design invites. Verdict: harmonizable as deliberate framework structure; a genuine contradiction only under a chronological-literalist construal the author probably did not intend.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Genesis 1 is built on a deliberate domain-then-inhabitant parallelism in which day one establishes the day/night cycle and day four installs the luminaries that govern it; the repeated 'separating' vocabulary (b-d-l) marks that structural correspondence rather than narrating two competing physical events. Read as the literary scheme its author designed, the repetition is intelligible and not a strict chronological contradiction, though it remains incoherent if pressed as sequential natural history.

entries.question: How many gods are there?
entries.books_in_tension: Genesis, Deuteronomy, 1 Kings, Isaiah, Mark, John, 1 Corinthians
entries.summary: Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and New Testament passages repeatedly assert strict monotheism, with YHWH alone and no other gods beside him. Genesis 1:26, 3:22, and 11:7 have God using first-person plural ('let us make,' 'one of us') and Psalm 82 has God judging in the assembly of gods. The Hebrew Bible carries both currents at once.
entries.commentary: The question is slightly coarse as posed, but the contradiction underneath is real and is one of the most important issues in Hebrew Bible scholarship. The later monotheistic texts, especially Deutero-Isaiah (40-55), are polemically insistent that YHWH is the only God. The older material is more complicated. Genesis 1:26's 'let us make man in our image' has been explained as the royal 'we,' as a plural of deliberation, as an address to the angelic court, or as a Trinitarian anticipation. Only two of those are serious. Hebrew has no royal plural of that kind, and Trinitarian readings are a fourth-century retrojection. The strongest reading, carried by Michael Heiser and Mark Smith alike, is that these plurals reflect Israel's older cosmology in which YHWH presides over a divine council of lesser elohim. Psalm 82 makes this explicit: 'God has taken his place in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment.' Apologists including Archer and Daniel Block argue these 'gods' are human judges or angels, never actual deities. The textual data pushes back hard. Deuteronomy 32:8-9, in the Dead Sea Scrolls and LXX reading, has Elyon distributing the nations to the 'sons of God,' with YHWH receiving Israel as his portion. That's a council of gods, not a list of judges. Smith and Collins read the biblical canon as preserving an evolution from polytheism through monolatry to full monotheism, with the seams still visible. That is a subjective call on some passages, but the raw textual evidence for pre-monotheistic Israelite religion is extensive.
entries.scholarship: Mark S. Smith, The Origins of Biblical Monotheism (Oxford, 2001), pp. 27-40, 135-148. Mark S. Smith, The Early History of God, 2nd ed. (Eerdmans, 2002), pp. 32-43. Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm (Lexham, 2015), pp. 23-37, on the divine council. John J. Collins, Introduction to the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed. (Fortress, 2018), pp. 112-115. Patrick D. Miller, The Religion of Ancient Israel (WJK, 2000), pp. 1-45. Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties (Zondervan, 1982), pp. 359-360.

And God said, let us make man in our image. Genesis 1:26

And the Lord God said, Behold, then man is become as one of us, to know good and evil. Genesis 3:22

Let us go down, and there confound their language. Genesis 11:7

commentary_out.commentary:
The question as posed is blunt, but the underlying issue — whether the Hebrew Bible speaks with one voice on the number of divine beings — is among the most consequential in the study of Israelite religion, and the texts do not in fact speak with one voice. The later stratum, above all Deutero-Isaiah (chs. 40-55), is uncompromisingly monotheistic: 'I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god' (44:6); 'I am the LORD, and there is no other' (45:5). Deuteronomy 4 and 6 and the deuteronomistic 1 Kings 18 reinforce this, and the New Testament (Mark 12:29, 1 Cor 8:6) inherits it. Set against this are the divine plurals and the council texts. Genesis 1:26 ('Let us make humankind in our image'), 3:22 ('the man has become like one of us'), and 11:7 ('let us go down') have God speaking in the first-person plural.

Four explanations of the plurals compete. (1) A royal 'we' — but Biblical Hebrew attests no such majestic plural for a single speaker, and this option is generally abandoned by Hebraists. (2) A plural of deliberation or self-address — grammatically defensible and favored by some, including conservative commentators, though it strains in 3:22's 'like one of us,' which compares the man to a plurality. (3) Address to the angelic/heavenly court — God announcing his intention before the assembled bnei elohim; this is the reading of many critical and some traditional scholars and fits the council scenes elsewhere (1 Kgs 22:19-22, where YHWH consults the host of heaven; Job 1-2, where the bnei elohim present themselves before YHWH). (4) Trinitarian anticipation — a Christian dogmatic reading that postdates the text by centuries and which even most conservative OT scholars decline to defend as the original sense. The serious exegetical contenders are (2) and (3).

The council reading draws strength from Psalm 82, which is explicit: 'God (elohim) has taken his place in the divine council (adat-el); in the midst of the gods (elohim) he holds judgment' — and proceeds to sentence those gods to die 'like mortals' (82:6-7), an oddity if they were merely human judges, since human judges already die. Apologists, including Archer and Daniel Block, argue that these elohim are human judges or, alternatively, angels, never genuine deities, preserving strict monotheism. The strongest piece of evidence against that reduction is Deuteronomy 32:8-9. The Masoretic Text reads that Elyon apportioned the nations 'according to the number of the sons of Israel (bnei yisrael),' but the older reading is preserved in the Qumran scroll 4QDeut^j (4Q37), which reads bny 'lhym (bene elohim, 'sons of God'). The Greek tradition splits at exactly this point: the best-attested Old Greek reading is angelon theou ('angels of God'), but a significant variant reads hyion theou (υἱῶν θεοῦ, 'sons of God'), attested in pre-Christian Greek witnesses associated with the Fouad-266 group, and it is this latter reading — 'sons of God' — that corresponds directly to the 4QDeut^j Hebrew bene elohim and is widely held to reflect the more original Vorlage. The form bene el ('sons of El') is not the scroll's actual text but the cognate divine-council phrase known from Ugaritic, which scholars adduce to illuminate the same conception. Both non-Masoretic forms point back to a divine-council Vorlage, with YHWH then receiving Israel as his allotted portion (32:9) — a tableau of a high god distributing the nations among subordinate deities, with YHWH as one of them receiving Israel. The MT 'sons of Israel' is widely regarded as a later theological correction smoothing out the polytheistic implication.

The critical reconstruction, associated with Mark Smith and Patrick Miller, sees a trajectory from an early period in which YHWH presided over (or was situated within) a pantheon, through monolatry (worship of YHWH alone while other gods are conceded to exist, as in 'who is like you, O LORD, among the gods?', Exod 15:11), to the full ontological monotheism of Deutero-Isaiah and later texts. On this view the canon preserves the seams of that development: the divine plurals and council scenes are fossils of the older cosmology, and Deutero-Isaiah's polemic is the mature endpoint. Michael Heiser shares the council reading of the textual data — he too takes the other elohim to be real spiritual beings and Deut 32:8-9 as a genuine council text — but, unlike Smith and Collins, he rejects the evolutionary polytheism-to-monotheism trajectory; he reads the divine council within a synchronic Israelite 'monotheism' of a distinctive kind, in which the lesser elohim are created beings who never rival YHWH's unique ontological status. So Heiser and the critical scholars agree on the exegesis of the council passages while disagreeing on the developmental conclusion drawn from them.

The harmonizing readings are not impossible for any single verse — 'judges' for Psalm 82 and 'deliberation' for Genesis 1:26 can each be argued — but they must be applied selectively and against the grain of the Deut 32:8-9 textual evidence to keep every passage monotheistic. Because individual passages genuinely underdetermine the question while the textual and comparative data lean toward an earlier non-monotheistic stratum, the matter is best classed as disputed. Verdict: disputed, with the weight of textual and comparative evidence favoring a developmental account.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Defenders read the divine plurals as a plural of deliberation or as address to an angelic court, and the 'gods' of Psalm 82 as human judges or subordinate angels, which preserves strict monotheism; critical scholars read the same texts as fossils of an older divine-council cosmology. The data underdetermine a single forced reading of every passage, but the textual evidence (notably Deut 32:8-9, where 4QDeut^j reads bene elohim against the MT's bene yisrael, with the LXX hyion theou aligning with the Qumran Hebrew) weighs heavily toward an earlier non-monotheistic stratum, so the matter is genuinely disputed rather than cleanly resolved.

commentary_out.change_summary: Clarified per audit that the LXX of Deut 32:8 splits between angelon theou and hyion theou, with the latter corresponding to 4QDeut^j (4Q37) bene elohim regarded as more original; confirmed the siglum and kept all six citations.

issues.problem: The commentary attributes a specific reading of Deut 32:8 to 'the Fouad-266 group.' Papyrus Fouad 266 (Rahlfs 848) is a 1st-century BCE LXX manuscript of Deuteronomy, but it is fragmentary and is not the standard witness adduced for the 'huion theou' reading at Deut 32:8; the principal Greek witnesses for that variant are minuscule 848's relatives and Origen/patristic citations, while the dominant Old Greek reading is 'angelon theou.' Tying the 'sons of God' Greek variant specifically and confidently to 'the Fouad-266 group' overstates the manuscript evidence and risks a miscitation of the apparatus.
issues.correction: Soften to: a minority Greek tradition reads 'huion theou' ('sons of God') against the majority 'angelon theou' ('angels of God'), and this 'sons of God' reading corresponds to the 4QDeutj Hebrew 'bene elohim'; avoid pinning it specifically to Fouad 266 unless verified against the critical apparatus (Wevers, Göttingen Deuteronomium).

issues.problem: Quotation 'God has taken his place in the divine council (adat-el)' is given in the body. The Hebrew of Ps 82:1 is 'ba'adat-el' ('in the assembly/congregation of El/God'); rendering 'adat-el' as the underlying phrase is acceptable but the prefixed preposition/article context could be clearer. Minor transliteration nitpick, not an error of substance.
issues.correction: Optionally note the Hebrew as 'ba'adat el' for precision; no substantive change required.

entries.question: What kind of animals may we eat?
entries.summary: The canon gives four different answers to what humans are allowed to eat. Genesis 1:29 gives a strictly vegetarian menu in Eden. Genesis 9:3 tells Noah after the flood that every moving thing that lives is now food. Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 pull the permission back and restrict Israel to specific clean species, banning pigs, shellfish, hares, camels, and a long list of others. Mark 7:18-20 and Matthew 15:11 then have Jesus declaring that nothing entering a person from outside can defile them, which Mark 7:19 glosses as 'thus he declared all foods clean.' Four mandates, four different scopes.
entries.commentary: Skeptics read this as four incompatible dietary rules in one book. Dispensationalists like Charles Ryrie and Robert Saucy read it as a single progressive revelation unfolding across four successive covenants: Edenic vegetarianism, Noahic concession to meat-eating, Mosaic restriction for Israel as a separated people, and Christian freedom under the New Covenant. Source critics read it as three or four distinct authorial voices that were never trying to speak with one voice in the first place. All three framings deserve to be on the table, because each one gets something right. The dispensational reading is internally coherent for believers, and it gives the right answer to the question of why the rules look different in different books. What it concedes under the surface, though, is exactly what the skeptic is pointing at: the rules change. 'Be a vegan' and 'eat anything that moves' are not the same instruction, and packaging the change as a covenantal stage-transition doesn't remove the shift, it just names it. From a critical-historical angle, the rules change because the authors aren't the same people. The Priestly vegetarianism of Genesis 1:29 is P's idealized picture of the peaceful original order, with humans and animals both eating only plants. P then accounts for real-world meat consumption with Genesis 9:3's post-flood grant to Noah, which is P again softening its own ideal. The Levitical kashrut of Leviticus 11 is Priestly and Holiness Code material doing systematic purity work, and Jacob Milgrom's three-volume Anchor Bible commentary on Leviticus walks through how the dietary restrictions function inside P's broader holiness logic. Deuteronomy 14 is a parallel but not identical list from the Deuteronomic legal tradition. And the Markan declaration is, by the nearly universal consensus of critical New Testament scholarship, a Markan editorial gloss. Joel Marcus in the Anchor Bible Mark 1-8 is explicit that 'cleansing all foods' (katharizon panta ta bromata) is the evangelist speaking, not a red-letter quotation of the historical Jesus. Jonathan Klawans's work on moral versus ritual impurity sharpens the point: the historical Jesus in Mark 7 is arguing that moral defilement matters more than ritual handwashing, not that kosher law is abrogated. The Markan community, writing decades later for a mixed Gentile audience, then universalized the saying. Ehrman's observation lands here too. If Jesus had actually cancelled kosher law during his ministry, the Jerusalem council debates in Acts 15 and Peter's rooftop vision in Acts 10 are incomprehensible as narratives — Peter wouldn't need a three-fold heavenly vision to convince him that Gentile food was clean. The harmonization reading works theologically if you're already committed to progressive revelation. The source-critical reading is parsimonious and explains the data without needing a covenantal scaffolding read back into the texts. That is of course a subjective call on the evidence, but the evidence points to multiple authors working out food law over centuries, not a single unchanging divine menu dispensed in stages.

answers.answer: Don't eat animals. Be a vegan (or at least a vegetarian).
answers.answer_explanation: And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat. Genesis 1:29

answers.answer: Only certain kinds of animals may be eaten.
answers.answer_explanation:
Nevertheless, these shall ye not eat, of them that chew the cud or of them that divide the cloven hoof; as the camel and the hare, and the coney; for they chew the cud, but divide not the hoof; therefore, they are unclean unto you. And the swine, because it divideth the hoof, yet cheweth not the cud, it is unclean unto you; ye shall not eat of their flesh, nor touch their dead carcass. Deuteronomy 14:7-8

These are the beasts which ye shall eat among all the beasts that are on the earth. Whatsoever parteth the hoof, and is clovenfooted, and cheweth the cud, among the beasts, that shall ye eat. Nevertheless these shall ye not eat of them that chew the cud, or of them that divide the hoof: as the camel, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you. Leviticus 11:2-4
Every moving thing that liveth shall be meat for you. Genesis 9:3

answers.answer: Eat whatever you want. Nothing is unclean, so there's no need to wash it.
answers.answer_explanation: And he saith unto them, Are ye so without understanding also? Do ye not perceive, that whatsoever thing from without entereth into the man, it cannot defile him; Because it entereth not into his heart, but into the belly, and goeth out into the draught, purging all meats? And he said, That which cometh out of the man, that defileth the man. Mark 7:18-20, Matthew 15:11

commentary_out.commentary:
The canon supplies four answers to a single question, and they do not say the same thing. Genesis 1:29 puts both humans and animals on a strictly plant diet in the original order. Genesis 9:3, after the flood, grants Noah 'every moving thing that lives' as food. Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 then retract that universal grant for Israel, permitting only animals that both chew the cud and part the hoof, and barring the pig, camel, hare, hyrax, and a long catalogue of sea creatures, birds, and swarming things. Finally Mark 7:18-20 and Matthew 15:11 have Jesus declare that nothing entering a person from outside defiles, which Mark 7:19 glosses with the editorial clause 'thus he declared all foods clean.' Four mandates, four scopes.

Three framings sit on the table. Dispensationalists such as Charles Ryrie and Robert Saucy read a single progressive revelation across successive covenants — Edenic vegetarianism, the Noahic concession to meat, the Mosaic restriction marking Israel as a separated people, and Christian freedom under the New Covenant. This reading is internally coherent and answers why the rules differ by book. What it concedes, however, is exactly the skeptic's point: the rules change. 'Eat only plants' and 'eat anything that moves' are not one instruction, and naming the shift a covenantal stage-transition labels it rather than dissolving it.

From a historical-critical angle the rules differ because the authors differ. Genesis 1:29 is Priestly (P), an idealized portrait of a peaceable original order in which no creature kills — a vision echoed in the eschatological peaceable kingdom of Isaiah 11. P then accounts for real-world meat-eating with the post-flood grant of Genesis 9:3, hedged immediately by the blood prohibition (9:4) — P softening its own ideal while introducing the first dietary limit. The kashrut of Leviticus 11 belongs to Priestly and Holiness Code material doing systematic purity work; Jacob Milgrom's Anchor Bible commentary traces how the distinctions function within P's holiness logic, tying the permitted/forbidden taxonomy to Israel's vocation to 'be holy' (Lev 11:44-45), and Mary Douglas read the clean/unclean taxonomy as a system policing categorical boundaries — animals that do not conform to their class's defining locomotion or anatomy are anomalous and therefore impure. Deuteronomy 14 is a parallel but not identical list from the Deuteronomic tradition; its catalogue of named clean game animals (Deut 14:4-5) has no counterpart in Leviticus 11, a divergence that itself signals separate hands working the same body of food law.

The Markan declaration is, by near-universal critical consensus, a Markan gloss. Joel Marcus is explicit that the participial clause 'cleansing all foods' (katharizon panta ta bromata) is the evangelist's editorial aside, not a quotation of the historical Jesus; Marcus also observes that Matthew, working from Mark, lacks the clause at the parallel point (Matt 15:17-20). Davies and Allison's ICC commentary on Matthew likewise treats Matthew's reworking of the pericope as deliberately retaining a more Torah-positive frame. Critics widely note this omission, and it is plausibly — though not as a matter of consensus certainty — connected to a more Torah-conservative redactional tendency in Matthew, a Gospel elsewhere notable for retaining Jesus' affirmation that not one stroke of the law will pass away (Matt 5:17-19). Jonathan Klawans sharpens the matter through the distinction between moral and ritual impurity: the dispute in Mark 7 concerns handwashing and the priority of moral defilement, not the abrogation of the kosher categories themselves. The historical Jesus argues that what comes out of a person defiles more than what goes in; the Markan community, writing decades later for a mixed Gentile audience, universalized the saying into a cancellation of food law.

Bart Ehrman's narrative argument is forceful here. Had Jesus actually abolished kosher law during his ministry, the Acts narratives become difficult to read: Peter would not need a threefold rooftop vision (Acts 10) to be persuaded that no food is unclean — and would not protest 'I have never eaten anything profane or unclean' (10:14) — and the Jerusalem council (Acts 15) would have no live dispute to resolve. The early church plainly did not remember Jesus having settled the food question; the very persistence of the controversy is evidence that the Markan gloss is a later interpretive development rather than a remembered ruling. This argument depends on taking Luke-Acts as preserving genuine memory of the early Jerusalem community's practice, which is itself a reconstruction, but it is a well-grounded one: the food-law controversy is independently attested in Paul (Gal 2:11-14; Rom 14), confirming that the question remained open across the first Christian generation.

The harmonization works theologically for a reader already committed to progressive revelation; it partially resolves the canonical tension by supplying a coherent storyline in which each mandate belongs to its own covenantal epoch. The source-critical reading is more parsimonious, explaining the divergences — and the editorial seam in Mark 7:19 — without retrojecting a covenantal scaffold. The evidence points to multiple authors working out food law across centuries, not a single divine menu dispensed in stages. Verdict: harmonizable as theology, genuine diversity of sources as history.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: A progressive-revelation / multi-covenant scheme renders the four mandates internally coherent for a canonical reader, but it does so by conceding that the dietary rules genuinely change across covenantal stages; the source-critical reading explains the same data as the work of multiple authors over centuries.

entries.question: When was Eve created?
entries.summary: Genesis 1:27 has God creating male and female simultaneously on day six, in the divine image. Genesis 2:20-22 has Eve created separately, after Adam has already named all the animals, by YHWH taking one of Adam's ribs and fashioning her from it.
entries.commentary: Same doublet as the 'male and female' contradiction, and it's really a subset of the larger Genesis 1 / Genesis 2 problem. The Priestly account in chapter 1 has humans created together as a single act. The Yahwistic account in chapter 2 has the woman formed after the man, after the garden, and after the animals, as the solution to the man's loneliness when no suitable helper is found among the beasts. Apologists read this as two windows on a single event, with Genesis 2 filling in the details of Genesis 1's summary. Archer, Currid, and Mathews all run this line. The problem, again, is that the two texts describe two fundamentally different creation events. Genesis 1's simultaneous divine-image creation and Genesis 2's rib-derivation aren't different angles on the same moment; they're different stories. James Kugel's observation is that Second Temple Jewish interpreters noticed this contradiction and tried to solve it through the Adam-and-Lilith legend, where Adam had a first wife created with him in Genesis 1 (Lilith), who left him, and Eve was then made from the rib. That legend is rabbinic invention, but it exists precisely because the two texts don't fit together in a straightforward reading. The redactor of the Pentateuch left both accounts standing, and the tension has been generating interpretive work for 2,500 years. That's a subjective call on how to read redaction, but the textual data supports the critical reading.
entries.scholarship: James L. Kugel, Traditions of the Bible (Harvard, 1998), pp. 72-82, on Second Temple interpretations of the double creation. Richard Elliott Friedman, The Bible with Sources Revealed (HarperOne, 2003), pp. 33-37. Claus Westermann, Genesis 1-11: A Continental Commentary (Fortress, 1984), pp. 158-172, 225-234. Phyllis Trible, God and the Rhetoric of Sexuality (Fortress, 1978), pp. 72-105. Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties (Zondervan, 1982), pp. 68-69. Alter, Robert, The Five Books of Moses (Norton, 2004), pp. 17-22, on the literary independence of the two accounts.

God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; 
				  male and female created he them. Genesis 1:27

answers.answer_explanation:
And Adam gave names to  all cattle, and to the fowl of the air, and to every 
				  beast of the field; but for Adam there was not  found an help meet for him. And the LORD God 
				  caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up

commentary_out.commentary:
Genesis 1:27 has God create humankind 'male and female' together on day six, both directly in the divine image. Genesis 2:20-22 has the woman created separately and later: after the man is formed from the dust, after the garden is planted, and after the man has named all the animals and found among them no suitable helper, YHWH casts him into a deep sleep, takes one of his ribs (tselaʿ), and builds (banah) the woman from it. The two accounts differ in timing (simultaneous versus subsequent), in method (direct image-creation versus construction from the man's body), and in the woman's relation to the man (co-creature versus derivative helper). This is a focused subset of the larger Genesis 1 / Genesis 2 doublet.

The apologetic reading treats the two as windows on a single event, with Genesis 2 supplying the detail that Genesis 1 summarizes. Gleason Archer, John Currid (in his study commentary on Genesis), and Kenneth Mathews (in the New American Commentary) argue this 'two perspectives' approach: Genesis 1 reports that male and female were created; Genesis 2 narrates how the female came to be, with the temporal sequence belonging only to the close-up. At its strongest the claim is that 'male and female he created them' need not assert strict simultaneity — it asserts that both were, in the end, God's creation — and that Genesis 2 fills in an interval the summary leaves unmarked. The reading also notes that Genesis 2 is selective and topical in arrangement (the planting of the garden, the naming of the animals) rather than a strict chronicle, and that ancient narrative did not always observe modern conventions of sequence.

The difficulty is that the two passages describe two materially different events, not two descriptions of one. Genesis 1's simultaneous creation of both sexes in the divine image and Genesis 2's sequential rib-derivation cannot both be literal accounts of the same moment; in Genesis 1 the woman exists from the climactic act of day six, while in Genesis 2 she demonstrably does not yet exist while the man names the animals and is pronounced still 'alone.' The 'it is not good that the man should be alone' of Genesis 2:18 is unintelligible if the woman has already been created simultaneously with the man — the whole helper-search presupposes her absence. The source-critical assignment — Genesis 1 to the Priestly writer, Genesis 2 to the Yahwist — accounts for the divergence as two independent creation traditions juxtaposed by the redactor, who, as Friedman notes, left both standing without harmonizing the timing. The vocabulary and theology diverge in concert with the differing names for the deity (elohim in ch. 1, YHWH elohim in ch. 2), a marker the source critics treat as diagnostic. Robert Alter likewise reads the two as deliberately distinct literary compositions rather than report and elaboration, observing that the final editor evidently valued each enough to preserve both intact despite their incompatibility.

The history of interpretation is itself evidence that the tension is real and was felt early. As James Kugel documents, Second Temple and rabbinic interpreters noticed the discrepancy and generated traditions to absorb it. One ancient strand read the two passages as describing two different women: a first wife created together with the man in Genesis 1, and Eve made from the rib in Genesis 2. The medieval Alphabet of Ben Sira crystallized this first wife as Lilith, who, created equal and simultaneous with Adam, refused subordination and departed — a legend whose whole reason for existing is to reconcile the simultaneous creation of Genesis 1:27 with the later, derivative creation of Genesis 2. A second ancient strand proposed that the original adam was an androgynous or double-faced being, later split into male and female; this motif is preserved in the rabbinic sources — Genesis Rabbah 8:1 and the discussions attributed to R. Yirmeyah b. Elazar in b. Berakhot 61a and b. Eruvin 18a — and is surveyed in Kugel's treatment of the early Adam traditions. The motive is again to square the two texts: if the first human was a single bisexual creature, then the 'male and female' of 1:27 and the later separation of the woman in ch. 2 can be read as one process. These traditions are post-biblical invention, but they testify that careful readers across two millennia could not simply harmonize the accounts by a plain reading; they had to add a narrative the text does not contain — a second wife, or a primordial bisexual being, or a temporal gap nowhere marked.

That an honest harmonization requires importing material absent from the text is itself the strongest evidence that the texts do not natively cohere. The two-perspectives reading does not eliminate the contradiction; it relocates it, by quietly granting that Genesis 1's 'male and female created he them' must mean something other than what it appears to say so that Genesis 2's sequence can stand. The most economical explanation remains that two independent creation traditions stand side by side, and the interpretive ingenuity expended over the centuries is the measure of how poorly they fit. Verdict: genuine contradiction; the harmonizations (including the ancient ones) supply material the text lacks.
